# Kestrel.js Releases

## v5.4.0-beta.2 (pre-release)

Released yesterday

- Experimental WebSocket router
- New `onError` hook for streaming responses
- This is a beta. Do not use in production.

## v5.3.1 (latest)

Released 2 days ago

### Fixes

- Fix a memory leak when a client disconnects during a streamed response
- Correct the `Content-Length` header for compressed static files
- Router: trailing slashes are now matched consistently

## v5.3.0

Released 2026-09-15

### Features

- Route groups with shared middleware
- `kestrel build --analyze` prints a bundle size report

### Breaking changes

None.

## v5.2.4

Released 2026-08-02

- Security: reject request paths that contain encoded null bytes

## v5.0.0

Released 2026-03-03

- New router and streaming responses
- Requires Node.js 20 or newer. Node.js 18 is no longer supported.
- Drops the legacy `kestrel.config.js` format; use `kestrel.config.ts`

## Supported versions

The current major version gets features and fixes. The previous major version gets security fixes for 6 months after a new major release.

Upgrading from 4.x? Read the migration guide before you start.

# Larkspur Maps API: Rate limits

Every API key is limited by the plan of the account it belongs to. Limits apply per key, not per IP address.

## Geocoding

| Plan | Requests per minute | Daily cap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free | 60 | 2,500 |
| Business | 600 | 250,000 |
| Enterprise | Custom | Custom |

The forward and reverse geocoding endpoints share the same limit.

### Batch geocoding

Send up to 100 addresses in one request to `POST /v3/geocode/batch`. A batch counts as one request toward the per-minute limit but every address counts toward the daily cap.

## Routing

Routing requests are limited to 100 requests per minute on all paid plans. Matrix requests with more than 25 origins or destinations count as 5 requests.

## Static tiles

Tile requests are served from the edge and are not rate limited, but they count toward your monthly tile quota.

## What happens when you hit a limit

The API answers with HTTP 429 and a `Retry-After` header in seconds. Back off and retry after that delay. Repeated violations for more than 10 minutes may lead to a temporary suspension of the key.

## Raising your limits

Business customers can request a temporary increase for planned backfills from the dashboard under Settings → Limits.

# Quillstack Status

All systems operational.

## Past incidents

### Degraded performance of the Public API and Webhooks

**Resolved** – Oct 21, 2026

Started: October 21, 2026, 14:05 UTC
Resolved: October 21, 2026, 15:40 UTC
Duration: 1 h 35 min

Affected components: Public API, Webhooks

Between 14:05 and 15:40 UTC, about 18% of API requests failed with HTTP 503 and webhook deliveries were delayed by up to 50 minutes. The cause was a misconfigured connection pool limit rolled out to one database cluster. We rolled back the change and replayed all delayed webhooks. No data was lost.

### Dashboard login errors

**Resolved** – Oct 9, 2026

Started: October 9, 2026, 08:12 UTC
Resolved: October 9, 2026, 08:31 UTC
Duration: 19 min

Affected components: Dashboard

Some users could not sign in with SSO because of an expired certificate on our identity provider integration.

### Delayed exports

**Resolved** – Sep 28, 2026

Bulk exports took up to 3 hours instead of the usual 10 minutes.

## Uptime (last 90 days)

| Component | Uptime |
| --- | --- |
| Public API | 99.93% |
| Webhooks | 99.95% |
| Dashboard | 99.98% |

Subscribe to updates by email or RSS.

# How we cut our cold starts by 60%

By **Mira Okonkwo** · October 3, 2026 · 7 min read

*Updated October 10, 2026: added the arm64 numbers.*

Last spring our p95 cold start on Tessel functions was 1.4 seconds. Customers noticed. This post walks through what we changed, in the order we changed it, and what each step was worth.

## 1. Measure the right thing

We had been measuring the time to first byte from our own region. Real users were spread across three continents, so we started recording cold starts from synthetic checks in nine regions. That alone changed our priorities.

## 2. Ship less code

Our function bundle was 38 MB, mostly from a PDF library used by one endpoint. Splitting that endpoint into its own function cut the bundle to 6 MB and the cold start by 400 ms.

## 3. Lazy-load the database client

The database driver opened a pool of 10 connections at import time. We now open one connection on the first query.

## 4. Move to arm64

On arm64 our cold starts dropped another 15%, and the bill went down too.

## Results

| Change | p95 cold start |
| --- | --- |
| Before | 1,400 ms |
| Smaller bundle | 1,000 ms |
| Lazy DB client | 700 ms |
| arm64 | 560 ms |

Thanks to Daniel Reyes for reviewing a draft of this post.

Tags: performance, serverless, arm64

# harborctl configuration reference

`harborctl` reads `harbor.yaml` from the current directory. Every key is optional; the defaults are listed below.

## server

| Key | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `server.port` | `8443` | Port the gateway listens on |
| `server.adminPort` | `9090` | Port for the metrics and health endpoints |
| `server.readTimeout` | `30s` | Time allowed to read a full request |
| `server.idleTimeout` | `120s` | Time an idle keep-alive connection stays open |

## client

| Key | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `client.maxRetries` | `5` | Retries for idempotent calls that fail with a retryable status |
| `client.backoff` | `200ms` | Initial backoff, doubled after each retry |
| `client.maxBackoff` | `10s` | Upper bound for the backoff |

## tls

| Key | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tls.minVersion` | `1.2` | Lowest TLS version accepted |
| `tls.requireClientCert` | `false` | Require mutual TLS |

## Example

```yaml
server:
  port: 9443
  readTimeout: 15s
client:
  maxRetries: 3
```

The example above overrides the defaults for a local test setup. Run `harborctl config check` to validate a file before deploying it.
